title: "It's time. Time for digital security.": An End User Study on Actionable Security and Privacy Advice
abstract: Digital security advice is the focus of much research, with unsatisfying results: End users do not follow experts' security advice, and users and experts struggle to prioritize existing advice. Several studies point out that users are overwhelmed by the amount of available security advice, and make recommendations on how to improve existing advice. Nevertheless, we still do not know how to effectively give security advice. Inspired by daily habit apps, we developed a set of 30 pieces of short and actionable advice, and the Security App, an Android smartphone app to provide this advice to end users, to reduce mental effort, and to build secure habits. We conducted a 30-day online end-user (N=74) study to evaluate whether the set of advice is actionable and meaningful to users, whether users adopt the advice, and whether the app has an impact on security awareness and behavior. Our results show that the app is an appropriate tool to provide security advice to end users. Participants perceive the majority of tasks as comprehensible, actionable, and useful, and we show that the app in fact introduces secure behaviors. Our results can serve as a basis for future research on security advice and creating secure habits, and the possibility to effectively teach secure behavior. Prior work found that security advice is largely stable over time [10], [13], but is often inconsistent or confusing [14], and difficult to prioritize [1], [3], [14]. In our study, we focus on the design of security advice. 2228 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Digital security advice is the focus of much research, with unsatisfying results: End users do not follow experts' security advice, and users and experts struggle to prioritize existing advice. Several studies point out that users are over- whelmed by the amount of available security advice, and make recommendations on how to improve existing advice. Nevertheless, we still do not know how to effectively give security advice. Inspired by daily habit apps, we developed a set of 30 pieces of short and actionable advice, and the Security App, an Android smartphone app to provide this advice to end users, to reduce mental effort, and to build secure habits. We conducted a 30-day online end-user (N=74) study to evaluate whether the set of advice is actionable and meaningful to users, whether users adopt the advice, and whether the app has an impact on security awareness and behavior. Our results show that the app is an appropriate tool to provide security advice to end users. Participants perceive the majority of tasks as comprehensible, actionable, and useful, and we show that the app in fact introduces secure behaviors. Our results can serve as a basis for future research on security advice and creating secure habits, and the possibility to effectively teach secure behavior. 1. Introduction Advice sources on digital security and privacy are plenty, and include the internet, friends and family, or the newspa- per [1]. The amount of available advice is overwhelming for users, and sometimes advice can be confusing or con- tradictory [2]. Thus, many users decide to trust their own assessment, or stop caring about security advice, because they think they are “not important enough to hack” [3], [4]. But even if users know how to behave securely online, they may not be able to avoid insecure behavior when reacting subconsciously [5]. In a world of stimulus overflow, we often have to react spontaneously, or react “by habit”. Habit apps can help people to adopt new, “desired” behaviors, and they are very common in health, fitness, or meditation [6]- [8]. However, habits are rarely considered in digital behavior change interventions [9]. The usable security and privacy community has worked on digital security and privacy advice, investigating reasons for adoption and rejection of advice, and “what makes good security advice” [2], [3], [10]-[12]. However, adoption of experts' advice remains low, and experts also fail to prioritize advice [2]. Thus, we argue that a new approach is needed that implements recommendations for “good ad- vice” from prior work, and presents digital security and privacy advice in a user-centric way. We therefore take expert-reviewed security and privacy advice, restate it to be actionable and feasible in 10 minutes a day, and deliver it to users in an app for a month, via the popular “habits app” concept. Contributions. We developed an Android application with daily tasks that implement actionable security advice. In a 30-day online controlled quasi-experiment, we evaluated the tasks and the impact of app use on security awareness and behavior, answering the following research questions: 1) Is the advice perceived as (a) comprehensible, (b) actionable, and (c) useful? 2) Does the app improve security awareness and behavior? 3) Is the app a promising tool for communicating security advice? We find that participants use the app, follow the advice, and improve their security behavior. We show that (a) the set of advice we created is perceived as comprehensible, actionable, and useful, and (b) our Security App helps com- municate security and privacy advice and improve security awareness and behavior. We therefore recommend further exploring the delivery of security and privacy advice in this user-centric format. 2. Related Work We discuss related work in three key areas: security advice, security behavior, behavior change, and habit apps, and usability, user behavior, and user experience. We also illustrate the novelty of our work. 2.1. Security Advice Prior work found that security advice is largely stable over time [10], [13], but is often inconsistent or confus- ing [14], and difficult to prioritize [1], [3], [14]. In our study, we focus on the design of security advice. 2228 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00100 defined criteria for good security advice: it should be useful, comprehensible, relevant, and effective [15]. Additionally, it should be likely to be accomplished by the user and not include too many limitations and drawbacks. Later, Reeder et al. focused on similar criteria from public awareness com- munications: advice should be effective, actionable, consis- a measurement approach for the quality of security advice [2], including the following criteria: perceived actionability (including confidence, time consumption, disruption, and difficulty), perceived efficacy, and comprehensibility. We use these criteria to scaffold and evaluate our presentation of advice. Design Guidelines for (Security) Advice. Although re- searchers identified criteria for good security advice, users struggle to follow advice [2], [16], [17]. Research suggest improvements for security advice [3], [12]: Advice should be simplified and explained, it should be straightforward, should contain step-by-step instructions, and avoid technical jargon while clearly explaining why following the advice is beneficial for user security [3]. Advice must neither be inconsistent nor confusing [14]. Reeder et al. propose to obtain a balance between generic and specific advice. While generic advice covers a larger scope, it sometimes requires certain skills and judgment that end users lack [14]. Researchers also suggest improving the communication of security advice: features and functionality of tools should be better explained; data protection outside of privacy policies should be highlighted, and advice credibility should be transparent [3], [12]. Zou et al. propose that experts should identify the most effective and actionable advice [12]. Beautement et al. rec- ommend taking the “compliance budget” into account when considering the amount of advice for particular users [18]. Therefore, the set of advice should be minimized, and highly valuable to users [3], [14]. Reeder et al. recommend customizing and tailoring ad- vice to users by identifying particular audiences and cus- tomizing advice for each audience rather than communi- cating the same set of advice to everyone [14]. Redmiles et al. propose personalized security advice based on users' costs, risks, and values [19]. A “one-size-fits-all” approach for all users can even be disadvantageous. It could lead to significant market and individual losses. The right way to limit the amount of advice might not be clearly defined yet, but as Herley et al. stated in 2014: more is not the answer [11]. Importance and Prioritization. Herley et al. state, “the correct course of action is seldom as clear as we might like” [11]. It is, e.g., unclear which advice topics are important and how to prioritize them [20]. Redmiles et al. illustrated that users and experts struggle with advice prioritization [2]. Besides, end users and experts disagree on the advice they recommend [10]. Zou et al. suggest that experts identify the most effective and actionable advice from each area [12]. According to Herley, users value the importance of advice from an economic point of view [20]. Further, Schm ¨user et al. highlighted that prioritization of security advice becomes paramount during a crisis, and lack of prioritization can cause overwhelm [21]. Advice prioritization is a prevalent problem well documented in research-also from an advice curator's perspective [22]. Sources of Security Advice. Advice communication is critical for users to follow it [14]. Ion et al. suggested communicating advice differently, more effectively [10], and Rader et al. proposed using stories for advice communica- tion [23]. Prior work has shown that users rely on several different sources when looking for security information. Websites are one of the most common sources of advice [1], [2]. Sources of security advice differ between users of different education levels: more educated people are more likely to report coworkers and government websites as sources [24]. An- other essential aspect is the credibility of the source: While some research suggests users rely on computer security pro- fessionals, recommending that security advice clearly state the author's qualifications in computer security [3], other work indicates that users also rely on advice from strangers in online forums for advice, indicating non-experts' strug- gles with finding reliable advice sources [25], [26]. 2.2. Security Behavior, Behavior Change, and Habit Apps The human-in-the-loop framework describes the process for communicating computer security information to users as a set of six steps: attention switch, attention maintenance, comprehension, knowledge acquisition, knowledge reten- tion, and knowledge transfer [27]. In this model, knowledge acquisition can be seen as a critical component of security behavior change [2]. Research into users' motivations and decision-making regarding computer security advice, illustrates that self- confidence influences user behavior more than actual knowl- edge and social considerations were trumped by individual perceptions [19], [28]-[31]. Users' decisions are rational from an economic point of view [11], [19], [20]. They consider risks and costs when deciding which advice to follow or not to follow, but they struggle to identify less obvious risks [19]. Users weigh benefits and risk perceptions and see the benefits of their decision higher [16]. Users' concerns are not always in line with their actual behavior. The privacy paradox describes that user-reported concerns regarding privacy often differ significantly from their actual behavior, which can, again, be explained, at least in part, by overwhelm [32]. Behavior Change. Behavior is an outcome of both con- scious and non-conscious processes. To change their behav- ior, users should be consciously motivated and habits as non-conscious behavior should also be taken into account when designing behavior changes [9]. Habits are defined as learned impulses to perform a particular behavior, triggered outside of conscious awareness by specific cues [5], [33], 2229
